newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU winter grain sowings disappoint, spring hope.
newsitem.headline: EU winter grain sowings disappoint, spring hope.

text.p: A smaller than expected increase in European Union winter grain plantings for harvest in 1997 may be due to wet weather in southern Europe but could be followed by higher spring sowings, producers and analysts said.
In a preliminary forecast on Friday, the EU grain trade organisation Coceral predicted a 2.6 percent overall increase in winter grain plantings to 24.77 million hectares.
An increase of four to five percent had been expected after the EU halved to five percent the amount of arable land farmers must set aside to be eligible for EU subsidies.

"The forecast looks on the low side," said an official at COPA, the EU farmers' lobby, noting increases in winter soft wheat plantings in major producers, France, Germany and Britain, of 4.7 percent, 4.0 percent and 6.0 percent respectively.
The French figure is rising constantly, the official added.
But Coceral put the overall increase in the EU winter soft wheat area at only 2.9 percent at 13.97 million hectares.

Other grain varietes showed even smaller increases with winter barley only 1.6 percent higher even after an upwards correction in the German area. Durum wheat sowings were up 1.8 percent but rye was down 1.7 percent.
The COPA official noted that in some countries, such as Germany, farmers had preferred winter rapeseed.
Coceral noted declines in winter plantings in Italy, where the soft wheat area was 7.0 percent lower, Sweden and Denmark while no figures were presented for snowbound Finland.
Italian farmers, who were hampered by wet planting weather could substantially raise spring sowings, especially of maize and soybeans, analysts said.
The COPA official added that in some cases data was based on seed purchases because a December area survey had not been possible due to the delay in sowings.
A Coceral official said that last year's figures had been used for Spain and Greece because new data was not yet ready.
Continuous rain during the last two months all over Spain has hindered planting. In southern Spain, farmers are having to resow some areas and this will not be completed before the end of February.
Although official Greek figures will not be available until March, unofficial data points to a 10 percent increase in the durum wheat area in some regions.
